summary: Benchmarking has traditionally used constant packet sizes, which show device capability but differ from real traffic. Tests with a mix of sizes (IMIX) are sometimes added. This informational document specifies a way, called the IMIX Genome, to describe variable packet size mixes so they can be reproduced.

plainLanguage.summary: Real traffic has big and small packets mixed together. This gives a recipe for describing the mix so everyone tests the same way.

questions: how to specify packet size mix for testing
subtitle: Specifying repeating sequences of packet sizes for realistic network benchmarking.

tldr.problem: Network benchmarks traditionally test with fixed packet sizes, but real traffic mixes small and large packets. Without a standard way to specify these mixed-size sequences, test results cannot be reliably reproduced or compared.
tldr.mechanism: The IMIX Genome encodes a repeating sequence of packet sizes as a short string using letters (a=64 bytes, b=128, c=256, etc.). Custom packet sizes and long sequences can be described with alternative methods like run-length encoding or proportions.
tldr.outcome: Testers can now document the exact packet sequence used in a test with a brief code like 'IMIX - aaafg' (three 64-byte packets, one 1280-byte, one 1518-byte), making results repeatable and comparable.

facts.label: Minimum sequence length
facts.value: At least one packet (though typically 4-10 per cycle)

facts.label: Custom sizes
facts.value: Can be any octet length, encoded as A-Z

today: RFC 6985 is Informational and remains the standard way to specify packet size mixes for benchmarking. Equipment vendors and test labs use IMIX Genome notation in their reports and test documentation. No competing standard has displaced it.

sections.title: From Fixed Size to Mixed Size Testing
sections.content:
Since the earliest benchmarking standards (RFC 2544), test labs have evaluated network devices with constant packet sizes: all 64 bytes, or all 1518 bytes. Constant size tests clearly show device capability—small packets test header processing, large packets test bit-processing capacity—but they do not match real traffic.

In actual networks, packets arrive in many sizes: web requests and responses, video frames, IoT sensor readings, DNS queries, and countless other applications each send packets of different lengths. Researchers and equipment vendors recognized that tests with a mix of sizes (called IMIX, for Internet Mix) reflect real-world conditions better. However, different vendors and testers used different mixes, and there was no standard way to describe or reproduce a mix used in a test.
sections.plainLanguage: Testers used to send only 64-byte packets, or only 1518. Real networks have both at once. They tried mixing them but had no way to say 'I used this exact mix' so someone else could repeat the test.

sections.title: The IMIX Genome: Letter Encoding
sections.content:
The IMIX Genome uses a simple letter encoding for standard packet sizes. Each position in the sequence gets a letter from a to j (and z for custom MTU sizes):

  • a = 64 bytes
  • b = 128 bytes
  • c = 256 bytes
  • d = 512 bytes
  • e = 1024 bytes
  • f = 1280 bytes
  • g = 1518 bytes
  • h = 2112 bytes (jumbo)
  • i = 9000 bytes (jumbo)
  • j = 16000 bytes (jumbo)
  • z = custom MTU (must be specified separately)

A sequence is written as 'IMIX - ' followed by the letters in order. For example, 'IMIX - aaafg' means: 64-byte packet, 64-byte packet, 64-byte packet, 1280-byte packet, 1518-byte packet, then repeat.
sections.plainLanguage: Short letters stand for packet sizes: 'a' is tiny (64), 'g' is normal (1518), 'i' is huge (9000). String them together to say what you sent.

sections.title: Custom Sizes and Long Sequences
sections.content:
Not every test uses standard sizes. For custom sizes, the tester defines their own code letters (A through Z) in a table, then writes the sequence using capitals. For example, with custom size A=50 bytes, the sequence 'CUSTOM IMIX - AAB' means three 50-byte packets.

When a sequence is very long or generated by a random process, the Genome notation becomes impractical. The RFC allows four alternatives: run-length encoding ('20 repetitions of abcd'), a table of proportions ('30% small, 60% medium, 10% large'), a deterministic algorithm ('increase by 1 octet each packet from 50 to 1500'), or pseudorandom generation with a seed and algorithm name.
sections.plainLanguage: You can invent your own sizes and give them letters. For really long sequences, just say the pattern (like '20 times this 4-packet mix') instead of writing it all out.

sections.title: Using the Genome in Test Reports
sections.content:
When a tester runs a benchmark, they document the source and destination addresses (or device ports), the IMIX sequence used for each pair, and other test parameters. They include the Genome string in the final report so anyone reading it knows the exact sequence that was tested.

Critical questions testers must answer: Is the IMIX sequence applied to each source-destination pair independently, across all pairs together, or in groups? The RFC suggests including this in a table alongside the IMIX code. This clarity enables other labs to run the same test and compare results.
sections.plainLanguage: In your test report, you write 'Between server A and B I used IMIX - aaafg.' Then anyone can repeat that exact test.

sections.title: Not a One-Size-Fits-All Standard
sections.content:
An important goal the RFC explicitly states is that the IMIX Genome does not standardize one or two 'official' IMIX mixes. The network is too varied—a smartphone network, a data center, and an industrial sensor network all have different traffic mixes. Instead, the RFC provides a language so each domain can specify its own mix clearly and reproducibly.

The RFC notes that there is no proven way to extrapolate results from one IMIX to another, even if they differ slightly. This is why documentation and reproducibility are essential: testers must use the same mix to compare results fairly.
sections.plainLanguage: There is no 'the correct mix.' Every network is different. This just lets you say what mix you used so tests are fair.
